prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat bands in twisted bilayer graphene at a magic angle and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in this tunable moire system

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is a new door: a single tunable device in which a twist angle and a gate voltage switch between metal, correlated insulator and superconductor. The chain of evidence is the kind the Physics Prize is meant for. The Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model of 2011 made a quantitative, falsifiable prediction. The 2018 experiments from Jarillo-Herrero's group then found the correlated insulators and superconductivity near that angle. Scanning probes and many independent groups have since reproduced and imaged the flat bands in several moire systems. Judged by the original-experiment test, the decisive original experiment is identifiable and verified, and the whole field of moire quantum materials follows from it. B046 also has the broadest support in the opening (all eight members ranked it, four in the top three). I hold that as a sign of shared judgement, not as proof of merit. After reading the colleagues' attribution arguments I now change my own set of names: I replace Andrei with Bistritzer, so that the 2011 prediction is credited to both of its authors.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is maturity and interpretation. The 2018 discovery is only eight years old, and the pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated, so the prize could be called early. A second reservation is attribution. Eva Andrei's STM work from 2010 onward showed twist-dependent van Hove singularities and flat-band signatures before 2018, and Cao, Fatemi and the 2018 co-authors did much of the bench work. Others (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) had earlier continuum-model theory. Three names cannot cover this history without leaving out real contributors. Against that, the existence of the correlated phases is not in doubt, and I would not wait for the mechanism, since the prize is for the discovery and not for the final explanation.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks topological insulators first. He values the clean Z2 mechanism, calls the field mature and arguably overdue, and would take Kane, Mele and Molenkamp while noting Hasan as a defensible alternative for the 3D strand.
responses.response: I accept the maturity argument for B028 and I ranked it fourth myself. My difficulty is attribution, not merit. The discovery has a 2D strand (Kane-Mele, then Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang, then Molenkamp's HgTe wells) and a 3D strand (Fu-Kane-Mele, Moore-Balents, Roy, then Hasan's ARPES). A three-name slate must leave out Hasan, who made the first 3D observation, as well as theorists missing from the credited list. I would ask whether the committee can be absolutely sure it has found the people who did the original work. That doubt is sharper here than for B046, where the prediction and the first observation are each tied to one clearly identifiable paper. I still treat B028 as the strongest fallback.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B046 second, reads the 2018 experiments as decisive, and says that omitting Eva Andrei's earlier STM evidence of flat-band signatures raises a fairness concern.
responses.response: I opened by crediting Andrei, so I take this seriously, and I wish to be careful. Her 2010 STM work on twist-dependent van Hove singularities was a real precursor, and the historical record should say so. But the criterion we apply is the original experiment, not the earliest related one. Her measurements did not show the magic-angle flat band with gate-tunable correlated insulators and superconductivity, which was the 2018 discovery. I therefore now agree with Kroll and most colleagues that Jarillo-Herrero, MacDonald and Bistritzer is the cleaner set. I will not use the committee's wish for more women among the nominees as a reason for the credit. That would be the wrong basis for a Nobel attribution. I do want the citation and the background text to record Andrei's contribution accurately.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B028 first and B046 second. He calls the prize possibly slightly early because the superconducting mechanism is unresolved, and he says that a three-person slate leaves out the Andrei and early-experimentalist contributors.
responses.response: I share the concern about prematurity, but I would separate two things. An unexplained mechanism is common in prize-winning discoveries. The high-Tc cuprates were recognised long before they were understood. What matters is that the observation is robust, and here it has been reproduced by many groups with several techniques. Where I do agree with Eriksson is that the 2018 co-authors, especially Cao and Fatemi, will be missed by a three-name limit, so the citation must be worded around the discovery and not around the people. I would also argue that this is a better reason for patience than for rejecting B046.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first. He regards it as a discovery-level advance in quantum optics, with every physical detail tested, and he notes the closeness to the 2025 circuit-tunnelling prize and the omission of Girvin and Huang.
responses.response: I take his point that circuit QED is a real discovery of strong light-matter coupling, not just engineering, and I appreciate his openness about his proximity to the field. I would still weigh it below B046 for two reasons. The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits makes a second prize for superconducting circuits so soon hard to defend. And the theory credit is incomplete for the reason he gives, since Girvin and Huang are not among the credited names. I am his Chalmers colleague, but I do not see that as a reason to defer on the physics. I would be glad to hear whether he thinks the circuit-QED step is independent enough from the tunnelling prize to stand without it.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first with Halzen as the single credited name and says the instrument-driven discovery is strong and mature. He also says a one-person award may be criticised as incomplete given the collaboration and earlier detectors.
responses.response: I like the instrument-first reasoning, and the diffuse astrophysical flux is verified and mature. But a prize for a collaboration-scale detector credited to one name is the hardest case of this kind for me. We need to be sure that the person credited is the one who did the original work, and the shortlist offers no other IceCube or AMANDA names to add. I would want the committee to settle who should be credited before I could support it. The detector concept, the first measurement and the source identifications were not all the work of a single person.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the unresolved pairing mechanism, and the eight-year age of the 2018 discovery, as making B046 premature.
Whether Bistritzer or Andrei is the better third name, and how much weight Andrei's 2010 STM work and the earlier continuum-model theory of Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto should carry.
Whether the 2D and 3D strands of B028 can be credited in one three-name prize without leaving out Hasan or the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang theory.
Whether B034 (optical lattice clocks) is seen as a new invention or a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with the shortlisted candidates is apparent from my profile. For transparency, I am a Fellow of the University of Tokyo (since 2025) and have long exchanges with Japanese microscopy communities, and Hidetoshi Katori (B034) is Tokyo-based, but I have no direct collaboration with him. My Chalmers colleague Goran Johansson sits on the committee and prefers B035. I have no co-authorship with anyone credited on the shortlist.
